### **Topics Taught by Siddharth**

### **Caching Fundamentals**
*   **Core Concept**: Caching is a critical technique in AI/ML to store frequently accessed data, significantly reducing latency and computational costs by preventing redundant operations like re-embedding or repeated API calls to LLMs.
    *   Siddharth explained that caching can reduce response times dramatically: "Because catches is usually 0.5 milliseconds. Embedding takes around 1 to 2 seconds." [2026-07-31, Page 9 — Siddharth Saminathan]
    *   He emphasized that caching addresses three main problems: "caching solves 3 problems, basically latency. And what is the last one? The." [2026-07-31, Page 9 — Siddharth Saminathan] and "it saves latency, and it saves cost." [2026-07-31, Page 9 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **Why Emphasized**: Siddharth stressed that understanding caching is a fundamental skill for any AI engineer, stating, "Caching, embeddings, how to, you know, save on embedding costs at scale. Those will be, these buttons will haunt you forever. As long as you are an AI engineer, in every interview they will ask you, okay?" [2026-07-22, Page 3 — Siddharth Saminathan]. He also highlighted its importance for user experience and scalability: "caching is not only for you, us for, it is for people who will be using whatever you're building in the future, and it is for people who are concurrently using it every day. And as that number grows, your cost must come down. That is the reason people implement caching, okay?" [2026-07-22, Page 3 — Siddharth Saminathan].

### **Types of Caching**
*   **Core Concept**: Siddharth detailed various types of caching relevant to AI/ML systems, including embedding caching, LLM caching, prompt caching, and KV caching, each serving distinct purposes.
    *   **Embedding Caching**: This involves storing the vector representations (embeddings) of documents or user inputs to avoid re-computing them.
        *   "You can do caching and embedding also." [2026-07-28, Page 5 — Siddharth Saminathan]
        *   Siddharth corrected Himaya's implementation, clarifying that the goal is to cache documents, not user input, to avoid re-embedding "800 points every time I ask a query." [2026-07-22, Page 2 — Siddharth Saminathan]. He explicitly stated, "you have cached the user input... I'm not sure why you have done that user input anyway, we need to embed it, so that is no point in caching it." [2026-07-22, Page 2 — Siddharth Saminathan].
        *   **Why Emphasized**: To ensure trainees correctly apply caching to reduce costs and latency associated with embedding generation, especially for large document sets.
    *   **LLM Caching**: Storing the inputs and outputs of Large Language Models (LLMs) to reuse previous computations for identical queries.
        *   Siddharth provided a use case: "I ask GPT, here is my user input. Give me a JSON. That contains. Emotions, entities, and posual links... If I have the same input again, I will not go and compute it from GPT. I'll take it from the cache." [2026-07-23, Page 9 — Siddharth Saminathan].
        *   He explained that LLM caching saves money over time: "maybe first year it will only save 5%, second year probably only 20%, but then as years go by it will increase and you will save a lot of money." [2026-07-23, Page 8 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **Prompt Caching**: Storing frequently used prompts to LLMs to avoid re-sending them, particularly useful for large, static prompts.
        *   "You can even cache your prompts in the in your LLM. Whatever LLM you're using, you can cache the prompts. That will also save costs." [2026-07-28, Page 5 — Siddharth Saminathan].
        *   Siddharth clarified its utility: "Prom cache is useful when you're trying to... make a lot of inference on a specific model using the same problem. If your prompts are changing, then there's no point in prompt caching." [2026-07-23, Page 9 — Siddharth Saminathan]. He also noted that prompt caching is server-side and not created by the user: "you don't create the bump cache, they already created it. We just we just can go and cache your prompts." [2026-07-23, Page 11 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **KV Caching (Key-Value Caching)**: This is an internal LLM mechanism that stores intermediate computations (keys and values) during the generation process, not just prompts.
        *   Siddharth distinguished it from prompt caching: "KV caching is entirely different. KV cache is whatever information that it's not just prompts, it's also whatever information that the LLM processes in that particular request or particularity." [2026-07-23, Page 9 — Siddharth Saminathan].
        *   He explained its function: "whatever the model has learned about you is there sitting here. KV cache. That is KB cache, so don't mix up these things. These are completely different things. Embedding cache is something that lives in your laptop or in your cloud server. This lives inside the app. You cannot create this in your laptop. Not possible." [2026-07-23, Page 11 — Siddharth Saminathan].
        *   **Why Emphasized**: To ensure trainees understand the distinct roles and implementation contexts of different caching mechanisms and avoid misapplying them.

### **Decision-Making for Caching**
*   **Core Concept**: Trainees must learn to strategically decide *what* to cache and *when*, considering factors like latency, cost, and the value of the information.
    *   "But you need to decide what you need to cache and what you don't need to cache." [2026-07-30, Page 3 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   Siddharth provided an example: "Let's say this JSON takes 3 or 4 seconds. I'll definitely cache it because three or four seconds I'm waiting, I'm making my users wait. So the next time any of them send the same number of words that I sent, it'll again take three to four seconds. I don't want it to take that time. I want it to be instant." [2026-07-30, Page 3 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   He also mentioned the constraint of cache size: "you can't magically cache everything in a way, because the cache has a size." [2026-07-30, Page 3 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **Why Emphasized**: To move trainees beyond simply implementing caching to making informed architectural decisions that optimize performance and cost-efficiency.

### **Chunking Strategies**
*   **Core Concept**: Chunking is the process of dividing documents into smaller, manageable pieces (chunks) for retrieval, and different strategies can significantly impact retrieval quality.
    *   Siddharth instructed trainees to compare strategies: "Why did you choose chunking strategy 2 over chunking strategy one? That is what you're trying to say. The whole exercise was for you guys to learn chunking properly, not retrieval." [2026-07-31, Page 8 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   He emphasized learning through experimentation: "you learn how to chunk, you learn what are the differences between the two chunkings, you learned it by actually performing it, actually, you did retrieval. Retrieval told you a story, and you learned that chunking strategy one is not good. That is learning number one." [2026-07-31, Page 9 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **Why Emphasized**: To highlight that effective chunking is crucial for retrieval accuracy and that trainees should understand the trade-offs and impacts of different strategies.

### **Metadata Filtering**
*   **Core Concept**: Metadata filtering is a technique used in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems to narrow down search results based on specific attributes (metadata) associated with documents or chunks.
    *   Siddharth explained its purpose: "Metadata filtering is there, so that retrieving can be easier whether you can find which in based on which metadata you is the fastest way you can find this particular information given a huge set of documents." [2026-07-28, Page 6 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   He clarified that metadata filtering does not directly reduce cost: "Metadata filtering does nothing to cost." [2026-07-28, Page 6 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **Why Emphasized**: To teach trainees how to improve retrieval efficiency and relevance by leveraging metadata, while also correcting misconceptions about its impact on cost.

### **Understanding Fundamentals and Asking Questions**
*   **Core Concept**: Siddharth strongly advocated for a deep understanding of fundamental concepts before implementation and encouraged trainees to ask questions when unsure.
    *   He observed a tendency to rush: "whenever I'm telling you some new thing to implement something, I think your brain, all three of your brains is immediately going to let me finish it, let me finish it, let me finish it. That is not how Things work, okay?" [2026-07-22, Page 4 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   He set a clear expectation: "I instead from today, I want all three of you to, you know, am I understanding what I'm doing? That is the only one question I want you guys to work with me. Okay, unless and until you don't understand stuff, don't implement it. Okay, if you don't understand it, come and ask me, I'll explain it to you." [2026-07-22, Page 4 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    *   **Why Emphasized**: To foster a learning environment where conceptual clarity is prioritized over rushed implementation, preventing future issues and building a strong foundation for complex AI/ML engineering. He noted this was a common issue even for senior professionals: "It happens to a lot of these senior people. It happened to me, it happened to Nihitha." [2026-07-22, Page 4 — Siddharth Saminathan].
